title: Mint Chutney
subtitle: Fresh herb and green chilli chutney
excerpt: Mint chutney (pudina chutney) is the bright green fresh herb sauce served with samosas, pakoras, and grilled meats at British Indian restaurants and throughout northern India. It is made by blending fresh mint, coriander, green chilli, lemon juice, and garlic into a smooth sauce. It takes 5 minutes and transforms almost anything it is served with.
sourceNotes: Pudina chutney is a staple of North Indian and Pakistani cooking, used as a condiment and dipping sauce. The British Indian restaurant version is typically smoother and milder than street-food versions in India.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in ice cube trays then transfer to a bag. Defrost as needed.
recipe.batchNotes: Scales directly. A large batch keeps for a week in the fridge.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps in the fridge for up to 5 days. The colour darkens slightly but the flavour remains good.

content.text: Mint chutney is simply blended fresh herbs, chilli, and lemon juice. The ratio that works best is roughly equal parts mint and coriander by volume, not weight: coriander is denser. A small piece of ginger, a clove of garlic, a pinch of salt, and enough lemon juice to get it moving in the blender. Adjust the chilli and lemon juice to taste.
Put all the ingredients into a blender or food processor with a generous pinch of salt and 2 to 3 tablespoons of cold water to help it blend. Blitz until smooth.
Taste and adjust: more lemon juice for sharpness, more chilli for heat, more salt if needed. The chutney should taste bright, herby, sharp, and pleasantly hot.

items.cause: Oxidation from the cut herbs, especially mint
items.fix: Add a squeeze of extra lemon juice, which slows browning. Store with a layer of cling film pressed directly onto the surface of the chutney to limit air contact.

items.cause: Too much water added when blending
items.fix: Add water a tablespoon at a time. The chutney should be thick enough to coat a spoon.

content.text: Mint chutney is the dipping sauce for samosas, pakoras, and bhajis. It also works as a spread on sandwiches and wraps (particularly with grilled chicken or lamb), and as a sauce stirred through yoghurt to make a raita. A spoonful stirred into plain yoghurt is the fastest raita.
